data: City street centerlines and High Injury Network
OpenDataPhilly parks, hydrology, art and historic districts
intro: Raasta finds the most scenic walk in Philadelphia, not the fastest one. Tell it your mood and how many extra minutes you can spare, and it builds a real route, then narrates it as you go.

A Python engine scores all 196,411 walkable street segments for trees, parks, water, public art and history. A language model turns your mood into weights, but it never picks the streets, and nothing can switch off what is dangerous.

title: Forested University
kicker: A university campus set inside a forest, from the aerial down to the atrium.
intro: A university campus set inside a forest. Seen from above, white buildings stand among the trees beside the water, with pink blossom along the paths that thread between them. One student housing block is pulled apart floor by floor, so the pines can be seen rising through every level.
At eye level the walkthroughs move through an atrium built around the trunks and along a street of brick blocks in winter. The visuals were built in Rhino and developed with AI image tools.

data: IM3 Open Source Data Center Atlas (PNNL), derived from OpenStreetMap
intro: Two interactive maps of the physical side of AI. Where AI Gets Built puts 1,472 existing US data centers on one map with the 34 new AI campuses already running and the 43 more that are coming. What AI Drinks lays the same campuses over the basins where water is already scarce: 39% of the new campuses sit in them.

Both are built in Python from the IM3 Data Center Atlas, Epoch AI's Frontier Data Centers list and WRI Aqueduct 4.0, and published as Mapbox GL pages with a floating card, hover details on every point and a legend that switches each layer on and off.
They are the first two studies in a series that follows the data centers into the water, power and climate risk around them. What AI Burns and Where AI Is at Risk come next.

data: Big Sur International Marathon course facts
City of Philadelphia footprints, parks and Heat Vulnerability Index
British Library, 1843 map via Wikimedia Commons
intro: Five static maps from the first week of the 30 Day Map Challenge, each one a question about a place answered with a number or a line. The Big Sur Marathon is drawn in plan and section with three line weights and one red line, the 510 ft climb to Hurricane Point. San Francisco's blocks are coloured by what the city lets you build: outside parks and public land, half of it is zoned for one or two family houses.

In Philadelphia, 12 towers now rise above William Penn's hat, all of them behind his back, and together they block 18% of his horizon. In the city's most heat-vulnerable tracts, 98% of streets are a ten minute walk from a park, but only 32% reach one of ten acres. Bombay's 1843 map of the seven islands carries today's shoreline in red.

Every map starts from the same Python toolkit, mapkit: the palettes, the credits and the title card live in one style file, each map is a notebook run top to bottom, and a publish step turns it into a live page and a thumbnail.

gallery.caption: Philadelphia Passes the 10-Minute Test. In its most heat-vulnerable tracts, 98% of streets are a 10 minute walk from a park. Only 32% reach one of 10 acres.

system.note: One style file holds the palettes, the credits and the title card. Every map starts from the same template notebook, and a publish step turns a finished notebook into a live page, a thumbnail and a caption stub, so a new map is one run away.
